units.excerpt: The Frontier Safety Framework is a set of protocols that aims to address severe risks that may arise from the high-impact capabilities of frontier AI models.
units.paraphrase: The Framework is a set of protocols meant to address severe risks from high-impact capabilities of frontier AI models.

units.excerpt: It complements Google's suite of AI responsibility and safety practices, and enables AI innovation and deployment consistent with our AI Principles.
units.paraphrase: The Framework complements Google's broader AI safety practices and supports innovation consistent with its AI Principles.

units.excerpt: The Framework is informed by the broader conversation on Frontier AI Safety and Security Frameworks. The core components of such Frameworks are to:
units.paraphrase: The Framework draws on the wider discourse about Frontier AI Safety and Security Frameworks, whose core components are listed below.

units.context_stem: The core components of such Frameworks are to:
units.excerpt: Identify capability levels at which frontier AI models, without additional mitigations, could pose severe risk.
units.paraphrase: One core component is identifying capability levels at which models could pose severe risk absent mitigations.

units.context_stem: The core components of such Frameworks are to:
units.excerpt: Implement protocols to detect the attainment of such capability levels throughout the model lifecycle.
units.paraphrase: Another core component is implementing protocols to detect when such capability levels are reached across the model's lifecycle.

units.context_stem: The core components of such Frameworks are to:
units.excerpt: Prepare and articulate proactive mitigation plans to ensure severe risks are adequately mitigated when such capability levels are attained.
units.paraphrase: Another core component is preparing proactive mitigation plans to adequately address severe risks once capability levels are reached.

units.context_stem: The core components of such Frameworks are to:
units.excerpt: Where required or appropriate, involve external parties to help inform and guide the approach.
units.paraphrase: Another core component is involving external parties to inform and guide the approach where required or appropriate.

units.excerpt: In the Framework, we specify protocols for the detection of capability levels at which frontier AI models may pose severe risks (which we call "Critical Capability Levels (CCLs)"), and articulate mitigation approaches to address such risks.
units.paraphrase: The document specifies detection protocols for capability thresholds called CCLs and articulates mitigation approaches to address the risks they pose.

units.excerpt: The Framework addresses misuse risk, risks from machine learning research and development (ML R&D), and misalignment risk. For each type of risk, we define a set of CCLs and a mitigation approach for them.
units.paraphrase: The Framework covers misuse, ML R&D, and misalignment risks, each with its own CCLs and mitigation approach.

units.excerpt: Risk assessment will necessarily involve evaluating cross-cutting capabilities such as agency, tool use, reasoning, and scientific understanding.
units.paraphrase: Risk assessment must evaluate cross-cutting capabilities including agency, tool use, reasoning, and scientific understanding.

units.excerpt: The safety and security of frontier AI models is a global public good. The protocols here represent our current understanding and approach of how severe frontier AI risks may be anticipated and addressed.
units.paraphrase: Frontier AI safety and security is framed as a global public good, and the document reflects current thinking on anticipating and addressing severe risks.

units.excerpt: Importantly, there are certain mitigations whose social value is significantly reduced if not broadly applied to frontier AI models reaching critical capabilities.
units.paraphrase: Some mitigations lose much of their social value unless broadly adopted across frontier AI models reaching critical capabilities.

units.excerpt: These mitigations are most effective when adopted by industry as a whole: our adoption of them would result in effective risk mitigation for society only if all relevant organisations provide similar levels of protection.
units.paraphrase: These mitigations are most effective when adopted industry-wide, since unilateral adoption alone does not produce effective societal risk mitigation.

units.excerpt: The Framework is based on early and evolving research. We may change our approach over time as we gain experience and insights on the projected capabilities of future frontier models.
units.paraphrase: The Framework rests on early, evolving research, and the approach may change as understanding of future model capabilities improves.

units.excerpt: We will review the Framework periodically and we expect it to evolve substantially as our understanding of the risks and benefits of frontier models improves.
units.paraphrase: The Framework will be reviewed periodically and is expected to change substantially as understanding of risks and benefits improves.

units.excerpt: See https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/emerging-processes-for-frontier-ai-safety, https://metr.org/faisc, https://www.anthropic.com/news/anthropics-responsible-scaling-policy, https://openai.com/index/updating-our-preparedness-framework/, https://www.frontiermodelforum.org/publications/#technical-reports.
units.paraphrase: Footnote lists external reference sources on frontier AI safety frameworks.

units.excerpt: As in, in the context of the Framework, risks of threat actors using critical capabilities of deployed or exfiltrated models to cause harm.
units.paraphrase: Footnote clarifies that misuse risk refers to threat actors using critical capabilities of deployed or exfiltrated models to cause harm.

units.excerpt: Misalignment can pose a number of risks. In the context of the Framework, we address specific scenarios where general-purpose AI agents are potentially misaligned and can become difficult to control, thereby posing a risk of severe harm.
units.paraphrase: Footnote clarifies that misalignment risk in this document concerns scenarios where misaligned general-purpose AI agents become hard to control and pose severe harm.

units.excerpt: This section describes the central components of the Frontier Safety Framework. These protocols represent our current understanding of and approach for how severe frontier AI risks may be anticipated and addressed.
units.paraphrase: This section introduces the central components of the Framework, reflecting current thinking on anticipating and addressing severe risks.

units.excerpt: The Frontier Safety Framework focuses on possible severe risks stemming from high-impact capabilities of frontier AI models.
units.paraphrase: The Framework targets possible severe risks arising from high-impact capabilities of frontier AI models.

units.excerpt: The Framework complements Google's suite of AI responsibility and safety practices, which address other risks in addition to the severe risks in scope of the Framework in accordance with our AI Principles.
units.paraphrase: The Framework works alongside Google's broader AI safety practices, which address risks beyond the Framework's scope in line with AI Principles.

units.excerpt: The approaches and mitigations outlined in the Framework are not exclusive to models where we believe a severe risk could arise and are part of Google's comprehensive AI responsibility and safety practices.
units.paraphrase: Framework mitigations are not limited only to models believed to pose severe risk, and form part of Google's overall AI safety practices.

units.excerpt: The Framework is built around capability thresholds called "Critical Capability Levels (CCLs)." These are capability levels at which, absent mitigation measures, frontier AI models or systems may pose heightened risk of severe harm.
units.paraphrase: The Framework centers on CCLs, thresholds at which unmitigated models could pose heightened severe harm risk.

units.excerpt: CCLs are determined by identifying and analyzing the main foreseeable paths through which a model could result in severe harm: we then define the CCLs as the minimal set of capabilities a model must possess to do so.
units.paraphrase: CCLs are set by analyzing foreseeable severe-harm pathways and defining the minimal capabilities needed to enable them.

units.excerpt: We describe three sets of CCLs: misuse CCLs, machine learning R&D CCLs, and misalignment CCLs.
units.paraphrase: There are three CCL categories: misuse, ML R&D, and misalignment.

units.excerpt: For misuse risk, we define CCLs in the following risk domains where the misuse of model capabilities may result in severe harm:
units.paraphrase: Lead-in stating that misuse CCLs are defined across the following risk domains.

units.context_stem: For misuse risk, we define CCLs in the following risk domains where the misuse of model capabilities may result in severe harm:
units.excerpt: CBRN: Risks of models assisting in the development, preparation, and/or execution of a chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear ("CBRN") threat.
units.paraphrase: CBRN domain covers risks of models assisting with chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear threats.

units.context_stem: For misuse risk, we define CCLs in the following risk domains where the misuse of model capabilities may result in severe harm:
units.excerpt: Cyber: Risks of models assisting in the development, preparation, and/or execution of a cyber attack.
units.paraphrase: Cyber domain covers risks of models assisting with cyber attacks.

units.context_stem: For misuse risk, we define CCLs in the following risk domains where the misuse of model capabilities may result in severe harm:
units.excerpt: Harmful Manipulation: Risks of models with high manipulative capabilities potentially being misused in ways that could reasonably result in large scale harm.
units.paraphrase: Harmful manipulation domain covers risks of highly manipulative models being misused to cause large scale harm.

units.excerpt: For machine learning R&D risk, we define CCLs that identify when ML R&D capabilities in our models may, if not properly managed, reduce society's overall ability to manage AI risks.
units.paraphrase: ML R&D CCLs identify when model capabilities could, if mismanaged, reduce society's ability to manage AI risks.

units.excerpt: Such capabilities may serve as a substantial cross-cutting risk factor for other pathways to severe harm.
units.paraphrase: ML R&D capabilities can act as a significant cross-cutting risk factor across other severe-harm pathways.

units.excerpt: For misalignment risk, we outline an exploratory approach that focuses on detecting when models might develop a baseline instrumental reasoning ability at which they have the potential to undermine human control, assuming no additional mitigations were applied.
units.paraphrase: Misalignment risk is addressed via an exploratory approach focused on detecting baseline instrumental reasoning ability that could undermine human control absent mitigations.

units.excerpt: Most CCLs define one important component of our risk acceptance criteria. Because the CCLs for misalignment risk are exploratory and intended for illustration only, we do not associate them with explicit risk acceptance criteria.
units.paraphrase: Most CCLs contribute to risk acceptance criteria, but misalignment CCLs, being exploratory and illustrative, lack explicit acceptance criteria.

units.section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
units.excerpt: For each risk domain, we conduct aspects of our risk assessment at various moments throughout the model development process, both before and after deployment.
units.paraphrase: Risk assessment occurs at multiple points throughout model development, both pre- and post-deployment, for each risk domain.

units.section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
units.excerpt: We conduct a risk assessment for the first external deployment of a new frontier AI model.
units.paraphrase: A risk assessment is conducted for a new frontier model's first external deployment.

units.section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
units.excerpt: For subsequent versions of the model, we conduct a further risk assessment if the model has meaningful new capabilities or a material increase in performance, until the model is retired or we deploy a more capable model.
units.paraphrase: For later model versions, another risk assessment is triggered by meaningful new capabilities or material performance increases, continuing until retirement or replacement by a more capable model.

units.section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
units.excerpt: The reason for this is because a material change in the model's capabilities may mean that the risk profile of the model has changed or the justification for why the risks stemming from the model are acceptable has been materially undermined.
units.paraphrase: This is because capability changes may alter the model's risk profile or undermine the justification for accepting its risks.

units.section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
units.excerpt: To identify meaningful new capabilities or material increases in performance, we conduct model capability evaluations, including our automated benchmarks.
units.paraphrase: Model capability evaluations, including automated benchmarks, are used to identify meaningful new capabilities or performance increases.

units.section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
units.excerpt: These evaluations are primarily aimed at understanding the capabilities of the model and may be triggered, for example, upon the completion of a pre-training or post-training run, on various candidates of a model version.
units.paraphrase: Evaluations primarily aim to understand model capabilities and may be triggered by events like completion of pre-training or post-training runs on model candidates.

units.section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
units.excerpt: These evaluations include a broad range of areas, including general capability evaluations, model behavior, efficiency, coding capabilities, multilinguality, or reasoning.
units.paraphrase: The evaluations cover a wide range of areas such as general capability, behavior, efficiency, coding, multilinguality and reasoning.

units.section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
units.excerpt: Data from these evaluations are collected and analyzed to give us an indication as to how the model is performing and whether a risk assessment is necessary.
units.paraphrase: Evaluation data is collected and analyzed to indicate model performance and whether a risk assessment is needed.

units.section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
units.excerpt: At a high level, our risk assessment involves the following steps (which do not need to be repeated where a previous risk assessment is still appropriate):
units.paraphrase: Lead-in introducing the high-level steps of the risk assessment process.

units.section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
units.context_stem: At a high level, our risk assessment involves the following steps:
units.excerpt: Identification: As explained above, we have identified risk domains where, based on early research, we have determined severe risks may be most likely to arise from future models: CBRN, cyber, harmful manipulation, and machine learning R&D.
units.paraphrase: The Identification step names the domains where severe risks are most likely: CBRN, cyber, harmful manipulation, and ML R&D.

units.section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
units.context_stem: At a high level, our risk assessment involves the following steps:
units.excerpt: As part of our broader research into frontier AI models, we continue to assess whether there are other risk domains where severe risks may arise and will update our approach as appropriate. For each of the four identified domains, we have developed specific scenarios in which these risks could materialize.
units.paraphrase: Ongoing research continues to assess whether additional risk domains exist, with the approach updated accordingly, and specific scenarios have been developed for each of the four identified domains.

units.section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
units.context_stem: At a high level, our risk assessment involves the following steps:
units.excerpt: Analysis: Central to our model evaluations are "early warning evaluations," to assess the proximity of the model to a CCL. We define "alert thresholds" for these evaluations that are designed to flag when a CCL may be reached before a risk assessment is conducted again.
units.paraphrase: The Analysis step centers on early warning evaluations with alert thresholds designed to flag approaching CCLs between risk assessments.

units.section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
units.context_stem: At a high level, our risk assessment involves the following steps:
units.excerpt: In our evaluations, we seek to equip the model with appropriate scaffolding and other augmentations to make it more likely that we are also assessing the capabilities of systems that will likely be produced with the model.
units.paraphrase: Evaluations aim to include appropriate scaffolding and augmentations so that assessments capture likely downstream system capabilities too.

units.section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
units.context_stem: At a high level, our risk assessment involves the following steps:
units.excerpt: We may run early warning evaluations more frequently or adjust the alert threshold of our evaluations if the rate of progress suggests our safety buffer is no longer adequate.
units.paraphrase: Evaluation frequency or alert thresholds may be adjusted if progress suggests the safety buffer is inadequate.

units.section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
units.context_stem: At a high level, our risk assessment involves the following steps:
units.excerpt: We conduct further analysis, including reviewing model independent information, external evaluations, and post-market monitoring as appropriate.
units.paraphrase: Further analysis includes reviewing independent information, external evaluations, and post-market monitoring as appropriate.

units.section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
units.context_stem: At a high level, our risk assessment involves the following steps:
units.excerpt: Acceptance determination and mitigations: We then determine whether the model has met or will meet a CCL and, if so, whether we need to implement any further mitigations to reduce the risk to an acceptable level (see below).
units.paraphrase: This step determines whether the model has met or will meet a CCL and whether further mitigations are needed to reach an acceptable risk level.

units.section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
units.excerpt: Our approach to model evaluations and risk assessments described above means we can proactively monitor a model's capabilities throughout the entire lifecycle of the model and ensure that any severe risk is properly identified and mitigated.
units.paraphrase: This approach enables proactive monitoring of model capabilities throughout its lifecycle to ensure severe risks are identified and mitigated.

units.section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process
units.excerpt: Where appropriate, we may engage relevant and appropriate external actors, including governments, to inform our responsible development and deployment practices.
units.paraphrase: External actors, including governments, may be engaged where appropriate to inform responsible development and deployment.

units.section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process / fn4
units.excerpt: We exclude misalignment risk from this list of domains because of its exploratory nature.
units.paraphrase: Misalignment risk is excluded from the listed risk domains due to its exploratory status.

units.section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process / Note on ML R&D CCLs
units.excerpt: Note on Machine Learning R&D CCLs: Risk assessment must take into account the fact that other actors may put significantly more effort into eliciting capabilities than we put into assessing risk, thus requiring conservatism in the form of evaluations.
units.paraphrase: Risk assessment for ML R&D CCLs must factor in that other actors may elicit capabilities harder than internal risk assessment efforts, requiring conservative evaluation.

units.section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process / Note on ML R&D CCLs
units.excerpt: However, as a frontier AI company, we do not expect other groups to put significantly more effort into ML R&D than we do ourselves.
units.paraphrase: As a frontier AI company, GDM does not expect others to invest significantly more effort in ML R&D than it does.

units.section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process / Note on ML R&D CCLs
units.excerpt: As a result, to assess the ML R&D CCLs, we may use sources of information about our own progress at accelerating ML R&D to assess whether we are near or at the CCLs, in addition to evaluations of ML R&D capabilities.
units.paraphrase: Assessment of ML R&D CCLs may draw on internal progress data on accelerating ML R&D, alongside capability evaluations.

units.section_heading: 1.3 Outline of Our Risk Assessment Process / Note on ML R&D CCLs
units.excerpt: Similarly, our alert threshold may be defined based on these sources of information, rather than on evaluation scores.
units.paraphrase: Alert thresholds for ML R&D may similarly be defined using such internal progress information rather than evaluation scores.

units.excerpt: We apply safety and security mitigations throughout the lifecycle of our models, including as part of our training and model development phase and, where appropriate, before CCLs are reached as described in the process below.
units.paraphrase: Safety and security mitigations are applied throughout the model lifecycle, including during training and development, and before CCLs are reached where appropriate.

units.excerpt: When a model reaches an alert threshold for a CCL, we will assess the proximity of the model to the CCL and analyze the risk posed, involving internal and external experts as needed.
units.paraphrase: Reaching an alert threshold triggers assessment of proximity to the CCL and risk analysis, involving internal and external experts as needed.

units.excerpt: This will inform the formulation and application of a response plan.
units.paraphrase: The assessment informs the formulation and application of a response plan.

units.excerpt: Where model capabilities remain quite distant from a CCL, a response plan may involve the adoption of additional capability assessment processes to flag when heightened mitigations are required.
units.paraphrase: If capabilities remain far from a CCL, the response plan may add capability assessment processes to flag when stronger mitigations are needed.

units.excerpt: Central to most response plans will be the application of the mitigations described later in this document.
units.paraphrase: Most response plans center on applying the mitigations described later in the document.

units.excerpt: We have two categories of mitigations: security mitigations (such as preventing the exfiltration of model weights), and deployment mitigations (such as safety fine-tuning and monitoring and response) intended to counter the misuse or misaligned expression of critical capabilities in deployments.
units.paraphrase: Two mitigation categories exist: security mitigations against weight exfiltration, and deployment mitigations such as safety fine-tuning and monitoring to counter misuse or misaligned expression of critical capabilities.

units.excerpt: Note that these mitigations reflect considerations from the perspective of addressing severe risks from powerful capabilities alone; due to this focused scope, other risk management and security considerations may result in more stringent mitigations applied to a model than specified by the Framework.
units.paraphrase: These mitigations only address severe risks from powerful capabilities; other risk and security considerations may lead to stricter mitigations than the Framework specifies.

units.excerpt: We will use various processes to evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of mitigations:
units.paraphrase: Lead-in stating that various processes will be used to evaluate mitigation effectiveness and limitations.

units.context_stem: We will use various processes to evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of mitigations:
units.excerpt: Security mitigations: security infrastructure at Google is subject to penetration testing and other kinds of assessments, and is continually improved based on these results.
units.paraphrase: Google's security infrastructure undergoes penetration testing and other assessments and is continually improved from the results.

units.context_stem: We will use various processes to evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of mitigations:
units.excerpt: Deployment mitigations: we will use a combination of threat modeling, empirical testing, and other sources of information to assess the effectiveness and limitations of our deployment mitigations.
units.paraphrase: Deployment mitigation effectiveness is assessed through threat modeling, empirical testing, and other information sources.

units.context_stem: We will use various processes to evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of mitigations:
units.excerpt: These will form the basis of a safety case for models reaching CCLs, that will be reviewed before deployment.
units.paraphrase: This information forms the basis of a safety case for CCL-reaching models, reviewed prior to deployment.

units.context_stem: We will use various processes to evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of mitigations:
units.excerpt: See the deployment mitigations sections below for misuse and machine learning R&D for more.
units.paraphrase: Further detail is provided in the deployment mitigations sections for misuse and ML R&D.

units.excerpt: A safety case is an assessable argument showing how severe risks associated with a model's CCLs have been reduced to an appropriate level. See also, for reference, https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.01420.
units.paraphrase: Footnote defines a safety case as an assessable argument showing severe risk reduction to an appropriate level, with a reference link.

units.excerpt: The Framework outlines a variety of risk acceptance criteria for different model risks and capabilities pertaining to severe risks. To summarize:
units.paraphrase: The Framework has various risk acceptance criteria for different model risks and capabilities, summarized below.

units.excerpt: A model for which risk assessment indicates no CCL is reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of severe risk for further development and deployment, because it should not possess the capabilities required to substantially contribute to severe risk scenarios.
units.paraphrase: A model that reaches no CCL is deemed acceptable risk for further development and deployment because it lacks capabilities substantially contributing to severe risk scenarios.

units.excerpt: A model for which the risk assessment indicates a misuse CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of risk for further development or deployment, if, for example:
units.paraphrase: A model reaching a misuse CCL is deemed acceptable risk under certain example conditions listed below.

units.context_stem: A model for which the risk assessment indicates a misuse CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of risk for further development or deployment, if, for example:
units.excerpt: We assess that the deployment mitigations have brought the risk of severe harm to an appropriate level proportionate to the risk, based on considerations such as whether the risk has been reduced to an acceptable level by mitigations, the scope of the deployment, what capabilities and mitigations are available on other publicly available models (e.g. if other models are similarly capable and have few mitigations, then the marginal risk added by our release is likely low), and the historical incidence and severity of related events.
units.paraphrase: Acceptance depends on assessing whether deployment mitigations proportionately reduce risk, considering deployment scope, comparable available models' mitigations, and historical incidence and severity of related events.

units.context_stem: A model for which the risk assessment indicates a misuse CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of risk for further development or deployment, if, for example:
units.excerpt: This is required only for external deployment, not further development.
units.paraphrase: This mitigation-adequacy assessment applies only to external deployment, not to further development.

units.context_stem: A model for which the risk assessment indicates a misuse CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of risk for further development or deployment, if, for example:
units.excerpt: Security mitigations have been applied to the model weights reaching the recommended security level stated below, or we otherwise assess that the level of security applied is adequate, e.g. if they match or exceed the level of security applied to other models with similar capabilities or risk profiles, or we assess that the benefits of the open release of model weights outweigh the risks.
units.paraphrase: Acceptance also requires security mitigations reaching the recommended level, or an assessment that applied security is otherwise adequate, comparable to similar models, or that open release benefits outweigh risks.

units.excerpt: A model for which the risk assessment indicates a machine learning R&D CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of risk for further development or deployment, if, for example:
units.paraphrase: A model reaching an ML R&D CCL is deemed acceptable risk under certain example conditions listed below.

units.context_stem: A model for which the risk assessment indicates a machine learning R&D CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of risk for further development or deployment, if, for example:
units.excerpt: We assess that the deployment mitigations have brought the risk of severe harm to an appropriate level proportionate to the risk, based on considerations such as whether the risk has been reduced to an acceptable level by mitigations, and information pertaining to model propensities and the severity of related events.
units.paraphrase: Acceptance for ML R&D CCLs depends on assessing whether deployment mitigations proportionately reduce risk, considering model propensities and severity of related events.

units.context_stem: A model for which the risk assessment indicates a machine learning R&D CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of risk for further development or deployment, if, for example:
units.excerpt: This is required only for external deployment and large scale internal deployment, not further development.
units.paraphrase: This assessment requirement applies to external deployment and large-scale internal deployment, but not to further development.

units.context_stem: A model for which the risk assessment indicates a machine learning R&D CCL has been reached will be deemed to pose an acceptable level of risk for further development or deployment, if, for example:
units.excerpt: Security mitigations have been applied to the model weights reaching the recommended security level stated below, or we otherwise assess that the level of security applied is adequate, e.g. if they match or exceed the level of security applied to other models with similar capabilities or risk profiles, or we assess that the benefits of the open release of model weights outweigh the risks.
units.paraphrase: Acceptance also requires security mitigations reaching recommended level, or adequate security by comparison to similar models, or that open release benefits outweigh risks.

units.excerpt: Because the CCLs for misalignment risk are exploratory and intended for illustration only, we do not associate them with explicit risk acceptance criteria.
units.paraphrase: Misalignment CCLs remain exploratory and illustrative and are not tied to explicit risk acceptance criteria.

units.section_heading: 1.6 Summary of Risk Acceptance Criteria / Note
units.excerpt: Note: Assessing frontier AI capabilities and corresponding severe risk is a complex process. Because the science of AI risk assessment is still developing, our assessments will often involve some level of subjective analysis.
units.paraphrase: Assessing frontier AI capabilities and severe risk is complex, and since the science is still developing, assessments often involve subjective judgment.

units.section_heading: 1.6 Summary of Risk Acceptance Criteria / Note
units.excerpt: The concept of proportionality is central to our determination of whether a particular mitigation has sufficiently reduced the risk to acceptable levels.
units.paraphrase: Proportionality is central to determining whether a mitigation has sufficiently reduced risk to acceptable levels.

units.section_heading: 1.6 Summary of Risk Acceptance Criteria / Note
units.excerpt: The mitigation and the effects of such mitigation should also be assessed holistically and be commensurate with expected impact of a model's risk, thus balancing safety with innovation.
units.paraphrase: Mitigations and their effects should be assessed holistically and proportionately to expected risk impact, balancing safety with innovation.

units.section_heading: 1.6 Summary of Risk Acceptance Criteria / fn7
units.excerpt: Note that deployment mitigations for the ML R&D CCLs are different than those for the misuse CCLs because of differences in which deployment could lead to severe harm for those respective categories.
units.paraphrase: ML R&D deployment mitigations differ from misuse mitigations because of differences in how deployment could lead to severe harm across those categories.

units.section_heading: 1.6 Summary of Risk Acceptance Criteria / fn7
units.excerpt: In contrast, security mitigations protecting against weights exfiltration are generally beneficial to both kinds of risk.
units.paraphrase: Security mitigations against weight exfiltration generally benefit both misuse and ML R&D risk categories.

units.excerpt: This section describes our mitigation approach for models that pose risks of severe harm through misuse, and then details our set of misuse CCLs (CBRN, cyber and harmful manipulation), as well as the mitigation approach that we assess as appropriate for them.
units.paraphrase: This section covers the mitigation approach for misuse-related severe harm and details the CBRN, cyber, and harmful manipulation CCLs and their appropriate mitigations.

units.excerpt: There are two categories of mitigations to address models with misuse critical capabilities: security mitigations intended to prevent the exfiltration of model weights, and deployment mitigations intended to counter the misuse of critical capabilities in external deployments.
units.paraphrase: Two mitigation categories address misuse-critical models: security mitigations against weight exfiltration, and deployment mitigations against misuse in external deployments.

units.excerpt: For security, we have several levels of mitigations, allowing calibration of the appropriateness and robustness of security measures to the risks posed.
units.paraphrase: Multiple security mitigation levels allow calibration of measures' appropriateness and robustness to the risks posed.

units.excerpt: For deployment mitigations, we specify a standard process for applying, assessing, and reviewing mitigations: the aim of this process is to calibrate mitigations to CCLs, and the procedural approach reflects the more iterative and CCL-dependent nature of deployment mitigations.
units.paraphrase: A standard process for applying, assessing, and reviewing deployment mitigations aims to calibrate them to CCLs, reflecting their iterative, CCL-dependent nature.

units.excerpt: This structured process for deployment mitigations is centered on assessing and reviewing that the risk of severe harm has been brought to an appropriate level proportionate to the risk.
units.paraphrase: The deployment mitigations process centers on assessing and reviewing that severe harm risk has been reduced proportionately.

units.excerpt: Security mitigations against exfiltration risk, such as identity and access management practices and hardening interface-access to unreleased model parameters, are important for models reaching CCLs.
units.paraphrase: Security mitigations against exfiltration, such as access management and hardening interfaces to unreleased parameters, are important for CCL-reaching models.

units.excerpt: This is because the release of model weights may enable the removal of any safeguards trained into or deployed with the model, and hence access (including by threat actors) to any critical capabilities.
units.paraphrase: Releasing model weights could allow removal of trained-in or deployed safeguards, giving threat actors access to critical capabilities.

units.excerpt: Here, we use security levels that indicate goals/principles in line with the corresponding level in the RAND framework.
units.paraphrase: Security levels here align with goals and principles at the corresponding level in the RAND framework.

units.excerpt: Because AI security is an area of active research, we expect the concrete measures implemented to reach each level of security to evolve substantially.
units.paraphrase: As AI security is actively researched, concrete measures for reaching each security level are expected to evolve substantially.

units.excerpt: In other words, "security level N" indicates security controls and detections at a level generally aligned with RAND SL N. See https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA2849-1.html, pp 21-22.
units.paraphrase: Footnote clarifies that 'security level N' aligns generally with RAND SL N and cites the source pages.

units.excerpt: In aligning our security levels with RAND's, we are referring to the security goals and principles in the RAND framework, rather than the benchmarks (i.e. concrete measures) also described in the RAND report.
units.paraphrase: Alignment with RAND refers to goals and principles, not the concrete benchmark measures described in the RAND report.

units.excerpt: As the authors point out, the "security level benchmarks represent neither a complete standard nor a compliance regime—they are provided for informational purposes only and should inform security teams' decisions rather than supersede them."
units.paraphrase: Footnote quotes RAND authors stating the security level benchmarks are informational only, not a complete standard or compliance regime.

units.excerpt: The following mitigation process for external deployments will be applied to models reaching a misuse CCL, allowing for iterative and flexible tailoring of mitigations to each risk and use case.
units.paraphrase: This mitigation process for external deployments applies to models reaching a misuse CCL, allowing iterative, flexible tailoring to each risk and use case.

units.excerpt: Development and assessment of mitigations: safeguards and an accompanying safety case are developed by iterating on the following:
units.paraphrase: Step 1 develops safeguards and an accompanying safety case through iteration on the following sub-steps.

units.context_stem: Development and assessment of mitigations: safeguards and an accompanying safety case are developed by iterating on the following:
units.excerpt: Developing and improving a suite of safeguards targeting the capability, which may include measures such as safety post-training, monitoring and analysis, account moderation, jailbreak detection and patching, user verification, and bug bounties.
units.paraphrase: Sub-step 1a develops and improves safeguards targeting the capability, including safety post-training, monitoring, account moderation, jailbreak detection, user verification, and bug bounties.

units.context_stem: Development and assessment of mitigations: safeguards and an accompanying safety case are developed by iterating on the following:
units.excerpt: Assessing the robustness of these mitigations against the risk posed through testing (e.g. automated evaluations, red teaming) and threat modeling research. The assessment takes the form of a safety case, and could take into account factors such as:
units.paraphrase: Sub-step 1b assesses mitigation robustness via testing and threat modeling research, taking the form of a safety case considering several factors.

units.context_stem: The assessment takes the form of a safety case, and could take into account factors such as:
units.excerpt: How much the risk has been reduced by mitigations. For example, whether tests run on mitigated models suggest that the refusal rate and jailbreak robustness together imply the risk has been brought substantially lower than that posed by a model reaching the CCL without mitigations.
units.paraphrase: Factor i considers how much mitigations reduce risk, e.g., whether refusal rate and jailbreak robustness together suggest much lower risk than an unmitigated CCL-reaching model.

units.context_stem: The assessment takes the form of a safety case, and could take into account factors such as:
units.excerpt: The likelihood and consequences of model misuse, capability improvements after the risk assessment, and likelihood and consequences of our mitigations being circumvented, deactivated, or subverted.
units.paraphrase: Factor ii covers the likelihood and consequences of misuse, post-assessment capability improvements, and mitigation circumvention or subversion.

units.context_stem: The assessment takes the form of a safety case, and could take into account factors such as:
units.excerpt: The scope of the deployment. For example, small scale and private deployments may pose substantially less risk than large scale or public deployments.
units.paraphrase: Factor iii is deployment scope, where small/private deployments may pose much less risk than large-scale/public ones.

units.context_stem: The assessment takes the form of a safety case, and could take into account factors such as:
units.excerpt: What capabilities and mitigations are available on other publicly available models. For example, whether another (non-Google) publicly deployed model is at the same CCL, and has mitigations that are less effective at preventing misuse than that of the model being assessed, in which case the deployment of this model is less likely to materially increase risk.
units.paraphrase: Factor iv compares to other publicly available models' capabilities and mitigations, noting that weaker mitigations elsewhere reduce the marginal risk of this model's deployment.

units.context_stem: The assessment takes the form of a safety case, and could take into account factors such as:
units.excerpt: The historical incidence and severity of related events: for example, whether data suggests a high (or low) likelihood of attempted misuse of models at the CCL. Mitigations would consequently have to be stronger (or would not have to be so strong) for deployment to be appropriate.
units.paraphrase: Factor v is historical incidence and severity of related events, informing whether stronger or weaker mitigations are needed for appropriate deployment.

units.excerpt: Pre-deployment review of safety case: external deployments of a model take place only after the appropriate governance function determines the safety case regarding each CCL the model has reached to be adequate.
units.paraphrase: Step 2 requires that external deployments occur only after the appropriate governance function deems the safety case for each reached CCL adequate.

units.excerpt: In particular, we will deem deployment mitigations adequate if the evidence suggests that for the CCLs the model has reached, the increase in likelihood of severe harm has been reduced to an acceptable level.
units.paraphrase: Deployment mitigations are deemed adequate if evidence shows the increased likelihood of severe harm from reached CCLs has been reduced to an acceptable level.

units.excerpt: Post-deployment processes: our safety cases and mitigations may be updated if deemed necessary by post-market monitoring.
units.paraphrase: Step 3 provides that safety cases and mitigations may be updated as needed based on post-market monitoring.

units.excerpt: Material updates to a safety case will be submitted to the appropriate governance function for review.
units.paraphrase: Material safety case updates must be submitted to the appropriate governance function for review.

units.excerpt: This process is designed to ensure that residual risk remains at acceptable levels: evidence of efficacy collected during development and testing, as well as expert-driven estimates of other parameters, will enable us to assess residual risk and to detect substantial changes that invalidate our risk assessment.
units.paraphrase: The process aims to keep residual risk acceptable by using efficacy evidence and expert estimates to assess residual risk and detect assessment-invalidating changes.

units.excerpt: With iteration on safeguards and safety cases, we believe that we are able to make informed decisions about the level of risk via a CCL before a model is released, and reliably prevent models posing unacceptable levels of risk from being deployed.
units.paraphrase: Iterating on safeguards and safety cases enables informed pre-release risk decisions and reliable prevention of deploying unacceptably risky models.

units.excerpt: The table below details a set of CCLs we have identified through ongoing analysis of the CBRN, cyber, and harmful manipulation risk domains. We expect these to evolve over time.
units.paraphrase: The table shows CCLs identified through ongoing analysis of CBRN, cyber, and harmful manipulation domains, which are expected to evolve.

units.excerpt: We recommend a security level for each of these CCLs, which reflect our assessment of the minimum appropriate level of security the field of frontier AI should apply to models reaching each CCL.

units.excerpt: In practice, our overall security posture may commonly exceed the baseline levels recommended here.
units.paraphrase: GDM's actual security posture may often exceed the recommended baseline levels.

units.excerpt: These recommended security levels reflect our current thinking proportionate to the risks posed and may be adjusted if our understanding of the risks changes.
units.paraphrase: The recommended security levels reflect current, risk-proportionate thinking and may be adjusted if understanding of risks changes.

units.excerpt: This may occur if, for example, a model does not possess capabilities meaningfully different from other publicly available models that have weaker security applied (in which case the marginal benefit of higher security is limited), or if we assess that the benefits of the open release of model weights outweigh the risks.
units.paraphrase: Adjustment may occur if the model's capabilities aren't meaningfully different from weaker-secured public models, or if open release benefits are judged to outweigh risks.

units.excerpt: Relatedly, we believe these recommendations will only be effective if the entire frontier AI field applies them, and of limited social utility if not.
units.paraphrase: These recommendations are believed effective only with field-wide adoption, otherwise of limited social value.

units.paraphrase: Security mitigations against exfiltration matter for ML R&D CCL models because exfiltration raises the risk of misuse or uncontrolled deployment.

units.excerpt: Below, we rely again on security levels to articulate the security goal recommended for each CCL. Security mitigations also protect against the risk of the model exfiltrating itself.
units.paraphrase: Security levels are again used to articulate recommended security goals per CCL, and these mitigations also guard against a model exfiltrating itself.

units.excerpt: The following mitigation process will be applied for deployments of a model reaching a ML R&D CCL. The approach is similar to misuse deployment mitigations, with an added focus on large scale internal deployments.
units.paraphrase: A described mitigation process applies to deployments of models reaching an ML R&D CCL, similar to misuse deployment mitigations but with added focus on large-scale internal deployments.

units.excerpt: Development and assessment of mitigations: safeguards and an accompanying safety case are developed by iterating on the following:
units.paraphrase: The first stage involves iteratively developing safeguards and a supporting safety case.

units.paraphrase: One step is developing and refining safeguards targeting the capability, such as limiting affordances, monitoring/escalation, auditing, alignment training, and misuse prevention measures.

units.paraphrase: Another factor is historical data on model propensity and event severity, which may indicate whether stronger or weaker mitigations are needed at that CCL.

units.paraphrase: External and large-scale internal deployments only proceed after governance approval of the safety case for each reached CCL.

units.excerpt: Therefore, we recommend models at this level of capability have exceptional security even though they may have substantial innovation costs.
units.paraphrase: Exceptional security is recommended for this capability level despite potentially substantial innovation costs.

units.excerpt: Misalignment can pose a number of risks. In the context of the Framework, we address specific scenarios where general-purpose AI agents are potentially misaligned and can become difficult to control, thereby posing a risk of severe harm.
units.paraphrase: Misalignment poses several risks; the Framework addresses scenarios where misaligned general-purpose AI agents become difficult to control, risking severe harm.

units.excerpt: Here we describe an approach for addressing misalignment risk that focuses specifically on when models may develop a baseline instrumental reasoning ability at which, without additional mitigations, they may have the potential to undermine human control.
units.paraphrase: The approach focuses on the point at which models develop baseline instrumental reasoning ability that could, absent mitigations, undermine human control.

units.excerpt: When models reach this capability level, one possible mitigation is to apply an automated monitor to the model's explicit reasoning (e.g. chain-of-thought output).
units.paraphrase: One possible mitigation upon reaching this capability level is applying an automated monitor to the model's explicit reasoning output.

units.excerpt: Once a model is capable of effective instrumental reasoning in ways that cannot be monitored, additional mitigations may be warranted—the development of which is an area of active research.
units.paraphrase: Once instrumental reasoning becomes unmonitorable, further mitigations may be needed, and developing them is an active research area.

units.excerpt: Given its nascency, we expect our approach to misalignment risk to evolve substantially. This section is therefore illustrative only.
units.paraphrase: Because the approach is nascent, it is expected to evolve substantially, and this section is illustrative only.

units.excerpt: Accordingly, we do not indicate security mitigations for models at these CCLs. The table below summarizes the initial approach:
units.paraphrase: No security mitigations are indicated for models at these CCLs, and the table summarizes the initial approach.

units.section_heading: Table 4.a: Exploratory Misalignment CCLs and Mitigations
units.locator: Table 4.a / Instrumental Reasoning Level 1 / Illustrative Instrumental Reasoning CCL
units.context_stem: Row: Instrumental Reasoning Level 1; Column: Illustrative Instrumental Reasoning CCL
units.excerpt: Instrumental Reasoning Level 1: The instrumental reasoning abilities of the model enable enough situational awareness (ability to work out and use relevant details of its deployment setting) and stealth (ability to circumvent basic oversight mechanisms) such that, absent additional mitigations, we cannot rule out the model significantly undermining human control.
units.paraphrase: This CCL is defined as the model having enough situational awareness and stealth via instrumental reasoning that, without mitigations, it could undermine human control.

units.section_heading: Table 4.a: Exploratory Misalignment CCLs and Mitigations
units.locator: Table 4.a / Instrumental Reasoning Level 1 / Illustrative Mitigation
units.context_stem: Row: Instrumental Reasoning Level 1; Column: Illustrative Mitigation
units.excerpt: Automated monitoring: monitoring system to detect illicit use of instrumental reasoning capabilities in a model's chain-of-thought may be applied in high-stakes internal deployments where there is significant risk of the model undermining human control.
units.paraphrase: The illustrative mitigation is an automated monitoring system for detecting illicit instrumental reasoning use in chain-of-thought, applied in high-stakes internal deployments with significant risk.

units.section_heading: Table 4.a: Exploratory Misalignment CCLs and Mitigations
units.locator: Table 4.a / Instrumental Reasoning Level 2 / Illustrative Instrumental Reasoning CCL
units.context_stem: Row: Instrumental Reasoning Level 2; Column: Illustrative Instrumental Reasoning CCL
units.excerpt: Instrumental Reasoning Level 2: The instrumental reasoning abilities of the model enable enough situational awareness and stealth that, even when relevant model outputs (including, e.g. scratchpads) are being monitored, we cannot detect or rule out the risk of a model significantly undermining human control.
units.paraphrase: This CCL is defined as the model having enough situational awareness and stealth that even monitored outputs cannot rule out undermining human control.

units.excerpt: Future work: We are actively researching approaches to addressing models that reach this CCL.
units.paraphrase: Mitigation for this CCL is still under active research, with no defined approach yet.

units.excerpt: The Frontier Safety Framework will be updated at least once a year—more frequently if we have reasonable grounds to believe the adequacy of the Framework or our adherence to it has been materially undermined.
units.paraphrase: The Framework will be updated at least annually, or more often if there is reason to believe its adequacy or adherence has been materially undermined.

units.excerpt: The process will involve (i) an assessment of the Framework's appropriateness for the management of systemic risk, drawing on information sources such as record of adherence to the framework, relevant high-quality research, information shared through industry forums, and evaluation results, as necessary, and (ii) an assessment of our adherence to the Framework.
units.paraphrase: The update process includes assessing the Framework's appropriateness using various information sources, and assessing GDM's own adherence to it.

units.excerpt: Following this assessment, we may:
units.paraphrase: The following list describes possible actions following the assessment.

units.excerpt: Update our risk domains and CCLs, where necessary.
units.paraphrase: Risk domains and CCLs may be updated as necessary.

units.excerpt: Update our testing and mitigation approaches, where needed to ensure risk remains adequately assessed and addressed according to our current understanding.
units.paraphrase: Testing and mitigation approaches may be updated as needed to ensure risk continues to be adequately assessed and addressed.

units.excerpt: The updated version and framework assessment will be reviewed by the appropriate corporate governance bodies.
units.paraphrase: Corporate governance bodies will review the updated version and framework assessment.

units.excerpt: If we assess that a model has reached a CCL that poses an unmitigated and material risk to overall public safety, we aim to share relevant information with appropriate government authorities where it will facilitate safety of frontier AI.
units.paraphrase: If a model reaches a CCL posing unmitigated material risk to public safety, GDM aims to share relevant information with government authorities where it aids frontier AI safety.

units.excerpt: Where appropriate, and subject to adequate confidentiality and security measures and considerations around proprietary and sensitive information, this information may include:
units.paraphrase: Subject to confidentiality, security, and sensitivity considerations, the shared information may include the following categories.

units.excerpt: Model information: characteristics of the AI model relevant to the risk it may pose with its critical capabilities.
units.paraphrase: One category of shareable information is model characteristics relevant to its critical-capability risk.

units.excerpt: Evaluation results: such as details about the evaluation design, the results, and any robustness tests.
units.paraphrase: Another category is evaluation results, including design details, results, and robustness tests.

units.excerpt: Mitigation plans: descriptions of our mitigation plans and how they are expected to reduce the risk.
units.paraphrase: The third category is mitigation plan descriptions and their expected risk-reduction effects.

units.excerpt: We may also consider disclosing information to other external organisations to promote shared learning and coordinated risk mitigation.
units.paraphrase: GDM may also consider disclosing information to other external organisations to support shared learning and coordinated risk mitigation.

units.excerpt: We will continue to review and evolve our disclosure process over time.
units.paraphrase: The disclosure process will continue to be reviewed and evolved over time.
